title: Two pregnant women (Luke 1:39–56)
hook: Mary hurries into the hills to Elizabeth, and the baby in Elizabeth's womb leaps for joy
carry: go to the one who understands
tomorrow: what Mary says back is a song, in the past tense. why?

segments.voice: Camp one ended with the Psalms and the line 150 doors. Camp two is the stories, and it opens where Jesus's story opens: with his mother, on the road.

You know that kind of news. The kind you type into the group chat, then delete. Type to your mom, delete. There's maybe one person who'd get it without a word of backstory. Mary has news like that. An angel has just told her she'll carry a child, and that her old relative Elizabeth, long given up on, is six months pregnant. So Luke says Mary goes, with haste, into the hill country of Judea. A long trip. Now she's at Elizabeth's door. She calls out a greeting. And before she can explain one thing about the angel…
screen: `NEWS YOU CAN'T EXPLAIN.` → `ELIZABETH, SIX MONTHS ALONG.` → `MARY GOES, WITH HASTE.`

segments.voice: Something happens first. In the Douay-Rheims Bible: "when Elizabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the infant leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost." The baby is John, the future John the Baptist, and Luke says he leaped for joy. Then Elizabeth cries out the words you learned on day ten: "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb." That's where the second line of the Hail Mary comes from. Look at who's in that doorway. Elizabeth is old; Luke says she and her husband Zachary were well along in years. Mary is young, unmarried and pregnant, with a story nobody will believe. Elizabeth doesn't ask for proof. She doesn't ask how. She blesses her. Then she asks, "whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" Here's one to tell a friend. In the book of Samuel, King David asked nearly the same thing about the ark of the covenant, and the ark stayed in that house three months. Luke says Mary stayed about three months too. It's one reason the Litany of Loreto calls Mary the Ark of the Covenant. Catholics call this scene the Visitation, the second of the joyful mysteries of the rosary.
screen: `THE INFANT LEAPED.` · `BLESSED ART THOU AMONG WOMEN.` · `SHE DOESN'T ASK FOR PROOF.` · `THREE MONTHS, LIKE THE ARK.` · then, large: `GO TO THE ONE WHO UNDERSTANDS.`

segments.voice: This one uses your phone. Think of someone who's waiting on news right now: test results, a job, a baby, a call that hasn't come. Send them one line that asks for nothing back, the way Mary walked in with nothing to fix. If you pray, you can pray for them by name as it sends.
Visitation. Mary in Elizabeth's doorway, a baby who leaped, and a blessing Catholics still pray.
The line to keep: go to the one who understands, and be that one when someone comes to you. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 22 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY DOES MARY SING IT LIKE IT'S DONE?`

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Visitation on May 31 and meditate on it as the second joyful mystery of the rosary; Elizabeth's greeting forms the second line of the Hail Mary.

notes: Luke 1:41–42 quoted from Douay-Rheims; confirm exact wording (DR spells Elizabeth 'Elizabeth'; Zachary for Zechariah).
Elizabeth described as Mary's 'relative' (Greek syngenis; often 'cousin' in older translations). Confirm.
Travel time from Nazareth to the hill country of Judea ('maybe several days on foot'): an estimate; the town is unnamed in Luke (tradition: Ein Karem). Confirm.
Trapdoor: the link between eskirtesen and David dancing before the ark is a common patristic and modern reading (Luke 1 and 2 Samuel 6 parallels); confirm.
Visitation feast: May 31 in the current Roman calendar (formerly July 2). Confirm.

v3: 'the first person to say blessed art thou among women' was avoided: in the Douay-Rheims, Gabriel also says it (Luke 1:28).
